title: Flick and the Rainbow Stone
markdown:
The blue mountains kept their own weather. Roads coiled along the ridges like sleeping snakes, and the air carried a chill that tasted of old stone. Flick lived in that frost the way other goblins lived in kitchens: always moving, always half a decision ahead of sense. Even when he sat, his eyebrows twitched, as if the next adventure might land in his lap if he only fidgeted hard enough. He wanted to be taken seriously. He wanted it so badly that he often started walking before he had finished thinking.

Smudge was the pause in that hurry. The jackdaw’s feathers were so dark they seemed to drink sound. He did not squawk for attention. He spoke in a timed wing-flick, a dropped twig, an unblinking stare that could halt even Flick mid-boast. On Flick’s shoulder he weighed almost nothing and somehow still felt like an argument.

Baroness Ophelia Von Fuzzington arrived on a morning that already had too much wind in it. The name alone made Flick’s toes curl inside his boots. She needed a guide to the hidden hot springs beyond the Whispering Peaks, a crossing that punished anyone who treated it like a garden path. Flick puffed his chest until the seams of his tunic complained and offered himself as the most capable guide in the region. The local elder, a mountain ram with a beard like a snowdrift, answered with one slow blink. Smudge cawed once, soft and doubtful.

“The path is quite straightforward, Baroness,” Flick said, already striding. He pointed at a narrow switchback that climbed as if it resented the idea of visitors. “Follow this, then a sharp left past those sparkly rocks. A simple stroll.”

Smudge nudged his ear. Sparkly rocks, in these mountains, usually meant magic that had not decided whether to stay put. A sharp left with no landmark was an invitation to walk a very long way in the wrong direction, especially for someone whose boots were made for lawns.

Flick was already around the bend, inventing the story of his triumphant return. “What marvels of engineering,” he called, too loudly. The echo came back thinner than he liked. The path crumbled under his hurry. Gravel went first, then a larger slide, clattering toward the Baroness’s gloves and her carefully composed face.

Smudge moved as if he had been waiting for exactly that stupidity. He caught a balanced boulder higher on the slope and shifted its weight by a feather’s worth. The worst of the cascade turned aside and settled with a thud that did not include anyone’s ankles. The Baroness looked at the jackdaw with the first unguarded surprise Flick had seen on her. Flick managed a smile that felt borrowed.

“See? Perfectly managed. Natural shifting.”

“Remarkable agility,” said the Baroness, cool as the wind. “And a most peculiar method for ensuring stability. Your jackdaw seems to take a rather active role in your guiding.”

Smudge preened. The silence did more damage than a lecture. Flick felt the boast settle on his shoulders and stay there.

They climbed. The blue of the mountains deepened toward violet, the colour the sky wears just before stars. Beneath the carved arches of Oakhaven Pass a market held a pocket of warmth: pine, roasting roots, goats, wool, dried herbs. From a stall piled with honeycombs came Beatrix Bumble.

She was an ogre. There was no polite way around the size of her. Her shoulders could have carried a cottage, and her hands looked as if they might crush stone by accident. The voice that came out of that shape was a summer rumble, low enough to make the jars on the stall shiver.

“Welcome,” she said. “Crisp air today. The sort that arrives before a good rain, when the world feels ready.” She set a small pot of honey in Flick’s palms. The surface held a captured scrap of sun. “For the journey. Sweetness steadies a hurried mind.”

Flick, who usually treated anything larger than himself as a possible emergency, found the panic failing to start. “Thank you. We are bound for the springs. I promised a smooth crossing.”

Beatrix’s eyes were old moss. “Powerful currents there, seen and unseen. Sometimes the strongest force is the one you do not try to control. Understand it. Let it go where it must, like water through stone.” She turned back to her bees. The calm around her did not ask permission. Flick tucked the honey away and, for once, did not fill the quiet with a better plan.

The gorge beyond the pass mixed river-sound with something that chimed like spells. Glint arrived first, robes like a peacock’s argument, and threw a waterfall of light down the canyon wall as if the rock had requested a performance. “Ephemeral beauty,” he announced, and waited to be scored.

Shimmer answered in midnight blue, silver motes knitting themselves into geometries that changed their minds mid-air. “Elegance,” she said, “is not the same as noise.”

They began awarding each other marks. Seven for form. Eight for dazzle. Nine for audacity. The Baroness’s polite smile thinned. Flick felt the temperature drop in a way that had nothing to do with altitude. From a ledge, Smudge rattled a run of sharp caws that Flick translated without effort: they are performing for themselves; she is about to decide the springs are not worth this; adjust.

He could not scold two spellcasters who would hear only goblin. He could not drag the Baroness backward without turning the whole escort into a retreat. Beatrix’s sentence sat in his mouth like the honey. He remembered shouting at a thunderclap when he was younger. The thunderclap had not been impressed.

Glint conjured shrieking griffin-shapes. Shimmer answered with silent beasts that used the shadows like corridors. The Baroness’s hands developed a tremor she was too well-bred to hide.

Flick breathed pine and the earth-sweet of the pot. Smudge nodded, a motion so small it might have been a trick of the light. Flick found, in his pouch, a smooth stone he had picked up near Beatrix’s hives. It still held a little of that stubborn warmth.

“You cannot improve a plan,” he said, and was surprised to hear the words come out level, “without first making it significantly stranger.”

He flicked the stone. Not at Glint. Not at Shimmer. At a wet slab where the afternoon sun was already doing a faint, unambitious rainbow. The strike was only a plink. The spray it threw caught Glint’s leftover sparks and the real light together, and the gorge filled with a thousand brief prisms, each one too small to compete and too many to ignore. Mist on the tongue. Damp stone. Colour that did not belong to either rival.

Glint and Shimmer stopped as if someone had closed a book. Their own work looked suddenly like practice.

The Baroness let out a breath that had been waiting since the gravel. “Oh,” she said. “That is quite something.”

Smudge offered one dry caw, the sound of leaves deciding to stay on the branch.

Flick held out his arm. “The springs are just beyond.” He did not explain the stone, or the honey, or the jackdaw’s earlier rescue. The spellcasters were looking at each other with the beginnings of respect, which was not the same as liking each other and would do. He walked at a pace a Baroness could match. The path held. The trees made the ordinary noise of trees, and for the first time that day Flick did not try to improve it.
characters: Flick (goblin who decides at startled-rabbit speed), Smudge (a jackdaw who speaks in wing-flicks), Beatrix Bumble (an ogre beekeeper with a surprisingly soft voice)
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, amusing fantasy story for older readers
author: StoryGen Community
